summary: Describes the timing issues in rolling a key in a DNSSEC-signed zone. It presents timelines and shows how parameters such as TTLs and signature lifetimes interact, so operators can change keys without breaking validation.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC key changes must account for records that resolvers have already cached. This RFC describes when to publish, use, and remove keys so that those records remain usable during a rollover.

questions: how long should a dnssec rollover take
what is a dnssec key rollover
subtitle: How to time DNSSEC key changes so cached keys and signatures remain consistent.

tldr.problem: Resolvers cache DNSSEC keys, signatures, and delegation records. If a zone changes keys before those cached records are safe to replace, validation can fail.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines rollover methods and timelines for Zone Signing Keys (ZSKs) and Key Signing Keys (KSKs), accounting for propagation delays and record lifetimes.
tldr.outcome: It recommends Pre-Publication for ZSK rollover, Double-RRset for KSK rollover, and standby keys to reduce delay during an emergency rollover.

today: RFC 7583 is an Informational document published in October 2015. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC describes its timing guidance as the state of thinking at publication.

sections.title: Why Rollover Timing Matters
sections.content:
A zone manager may need to replace a DNSSEC key after a compromise or as part of a management policy. DNSKEY, DS, and RRSIG records can be cached by resolvers, so the old and new information must remain consistent while the change takes effect.

A Zone Signing Key (ZSK) signs data within a zone. A Key Signing Key (KSK) signs the DNSKEY record set and is linked to the parent zone through a DS record. This RFC describes the timing of those rollovers; it does not cover algorithm changes or changes to TTL values.
sections.plainLanguage: Resolvers keep copies of DNSSEC records for a period of time. A zone must change keys in an order that keeps both old and new copies usable while caches update.

sections.title: Key Rollover Methods
sections.content:
For a ZSK, Pre-Publication adds the new key first, waits for cached DNSKEY records to expire, then changes the signatures and later removes the old key. Double-Signature publishes signatures from both keys before removing the old key and signatures. The RFC also describes Double-RRSIG, which changes signatures before introducing the new key.

For a KSK, Double-KSK changes the key before changing the DS record in the parent. Double-DS changes the DS record first. Double-RRset publishes the new DNSKEY and DS information in parallel, then removes the old information after caches have had time to update.
sections.plainLanguage: Each method keeps some old and new records available at the same time. ZSK methods manage signatures within the zone; KSK methods must also coordinate the DS record in the parent zone.

sections.title: Timing a ZSK Rollover
sections.content:
With Pre-Publication, the new ZSK is published before it signs records. The publication interval is Ipub = Dprp + TTLkey, where propagation delay accounts for changes reaching nameservers and TTLkey is the DNSKEY record lifetime. Once the old key stops signing, it remains published until signatures made with it have expired from caches.

The retire interval is Iret = Dsgn + Dprp + TTLsig. It allows time to sign the zone with the new key, propagate the changes, and let old signatures expire. Only after that interval is the old key dead and safe to remove.
sections.plainLanguage: Publish the new ZSK and wait for resolvers to learn it before using it. Keep the old key until old signatures have expired from caches, then remove it.

sections.title: Timing a KSK Rollover
sections.content:
A KSK rollover involves a parent zone because the parent publishes the DS record that establishes trust in the child zone's key. In the Double-KSK method, the new DNSKEY appears first; the DS record is then submitted to the parent, and the old key stays until old DS information has expired from caches.

The parent controls when a submitted DS record appears, so the zone manager may need to wait longer than planned. The Double-RRset method publishes the new DNSKEY and DS records in parallel and is described by the RFC as the most efficient KSK method. Where resolvers use RFC 5011 trust anchors, additional publish and revoke intervals apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A KSK change also depends on the parent zone publishing a new DS record. The rollover must wait for that change and for old cached records to expire.

sections.title: Standby Keys and the RFC's Recommendations
sections.content:
A key must be ready before it can be used to sign. Keeping a standby key in the ready state can therefore shorten an emergency rollover after a key is suspected of being compromised. For a standby KSK, the DNSKEY record set also needs to be signed with that key for the standby to save time.

The RFC generally prefers Pre-Publication for ZSKs and Double-RRset for KSKs. It says its timing guidance does not introduce security issues beyond those already discussed in the DNSSEC specifications it cites.
sections.plainLanguage: A standby key can reduce the wait before a replacement begins signing. The RFC recommends different rollover methods for ZSKs and KSKs because they depend on different records.
